reconcile.connective: JFB reads the proverb's peace-promise as a general rule that has always carried persecution for godliness as its standing exception.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptic's Annotated Bible catalogs this exact pairing, asking how a promise of peace with enemies squares with guaranteed persecution.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, Skeptic's Annotated Bible (1999), contra/no_enemies.html

excerpts.on_tension_rationale: JFB explicitly excepts persecution from the peace-with-enemies promise, directly answering the tension with 2 Timothy 3:12's guarantee of persecution for the godly.

pd_work.resource: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown, Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible (1871)
pd_work.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
pd_work.note: JFB treats this exact passage directly, glossing Proverbs 16:7's peace-promise with an explicit persecution exception; Haley's Alleged Discrepancies (1874) does not treat this pairing (verified: no hit for Proverbs 16:7, 'enemies,' or 2 Timothy 3:12 in the full archive.org djvu text).

link.title: 2 Timothy 3:12—Are all who live godly lives persecuted, or only some?
link.note: live apologetic treatment explicitly quoting Proverbs 16:7 against 2 Timothy 3:12 and arguing neither is a universal absolute
